title: Neither do I condemn thee
hook: a woman is brought for stoning, and the crowd leaves one by one (John 8:1–11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer from the cross. Your line was they know not. Whose blind spot did you try to see? Today, a crowd ready to stone a woman, and a man writing on the ground. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

What should happen to her? That's the question put to Jesus early one morning in the temple, where he's sitting and teaching, with people gathered around. Some scribes and Pharisees, John's Gospel says, bring a woman and set her in the middle. Caught in adultery, they say, in the very act. The law of Moses says such a person should be stoned. What do you say? The text is plain that it's a trap: any answer can be used against him. Everyone is watching. The woman stands there alone. And Jesus doesn't answer. He bends down and starts writing on the ground with his finger. Today: neither do I condemn thee.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE MIDDLE.` → `A QUESTION THAT'S A TRAP.` → `HE WRITES ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. They keep pressing him, and he keeps writing. John never tells us what he wrote. People have guessed, and the text simply doesn't say. What it does show is a man refusing to be rushed into a verdict. Second, the sentence. Finally he stands up and says, in the King James words: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he bends down and writes again. He doesn't argue the law. He doesn't defend her. He turns the question from her to them, and then looks down again, as if to give them room. Third, the leaving. The text says that those who heard it, "being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last." The eldest first. Maybe the ones with the longest memories of their own mistakes. One by one, they go, until only two people are left in that circle. Fourth, the last words. Jesus looks up and asks: "Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?" She says, "No man, Lord." And he says: "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." Both halves matter. He doesn't pretend nothing happened; he tells her to go and live differently. But he will not throw the stone, and he sends her out with a future instead of a sentence. Some Christians hear this story as a picture of mercy that is neither cheap nor cruel. The scene ends on a question worth carrying: which stone am I still holding, and what would it take to put it down?
screen: `HE WRITES, AND WAITS.` · `WITHOUT SIN? CAST THE FIRST STONE.` · `ONE BY ONE, THE ELDEST FIRST.` · `NO CONDEMNING, AND A FUTURE.` · then, large: `NEITHER DO I CONDEMN THEE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest open in your lap. Find one judgment you've been holding about someone. A verdict you've already passed: on a relative, a coworker, someone in the news, maybe yourself. Feel its weight, like a stone in the palm. Now ask the question from the story, gently, with no blame: am I without anything like this myself? Then imagine your fingers loosening, and the stone dropping to the ground. You can still think something was wrong. You're only putting down the throwing. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Neither do I condemn thee. Jesus's words to the woman left standing when every accuser had walked away, followed by go, and sin no more. Today's word.
screen: `NEITHER DO I CONDEMN THEE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: put down the stone. Today, catch one judgment as it forms, about someone in front of you or on a screen, and drop it before you throw it. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Christians read the story of the woman taken in adultery from John 8 as a picture of mercy joined to a call to change.

fork.setup: they bring a woman into the circle and ask Jesus: the law says stone her, what do you say? it's a trap. what does he do first?
options: bends down and writes on the ground.
fork.reveal: he stoops and writes with his finger, and only after they keep asking does he say, "he that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her."

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about not judging people.
what it means: mercy that refuses to throw the stone and still sends her out to live differently.
what a scholar hears: the eldest leave first, and the scene ends with two people in the circle and a mystery nobody can solve: what he wrote.

notes: Manuscript note deliberately left out of the voice: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some early manuscripts and is bracketed in many modern editions. A Keeper should decide whether to mention it.
'Some scribes and Pharisees, John's Gospel says': named because the text names them; the voice frames the accusers as a crowd and avoids making Pharisees a foil. Confirm the framing.
'Maybe the ones with the longest memories of their own mistakes' is offered as a guess, not a reading of the text.
KJV 8:10 includes 'and saw none but the woman'; quoted text starts at 'Woman', which is exact.
John 8:6 says the question was asked 'tempting him, that they might have to accuse him', which supports calling it a trap.
Editor pass: hook opener varied (third scene opener in a row); 'stones in their hands' and 'push/drags' cut (the text says brought); 'for anyone' stock close varied; John 8:10 ref corrected.
